newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Long-awaited Cyprus talks expected on July 9.
newsitem.headline: Long-awaited Cyprus talks expected on July 9.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan tentatively set a July 9 date to convene face-to-face talks between leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, his spokesman said on Thursday.
The talks would be the first known encounter in nearly three years between Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

U.N. Spokesman Fred Eckhard said invitations to the participants had not yet been sent out but Annan would propose the July 9 date. The negotiations are expected to be at a New York suburban area but a location has not yet been fixed.
"The venue has not yet been firmed up. It will be here, in the New York area," Eckhard said.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took over the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. The United Nations has been trying to reunite the Greek and Turkish Cypriots under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federal system.
If the initial talks go well, Annan has said he hoped to hold two more sessions that would indicate by September whether progress could be made.

Greece's deputy foreign minister, Yannos Kranidiotis, visiting the United Nations on Tuesday, was not optimistic about a positive outcome for the talks, saying little common ground had been found in so-called "proximity" or separate talks between U.N. officials and Cypriot leaders so far. He contended that Turkey had made few concessions.

An application by Cyprus to join the European Union has served as a new incentive for a solution to the problem since negotiations with the EU would be more complicated if the island remained partitioned.
The United States, Britain and other interested parties have stepped up efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem and appointed special envoys.

Peace efforts suffered a serious setback last year after four Greek Cypriots were killed by Turks or Turkish Cypriots along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone separating the two communities and the fatal shooting of a Turkish Cypriot sentry and the wounding of another.
A U.N. force has been stationed in Cyprus since 1964 after the breakup of a government in which both Greek and Turkish Cypriots took part following independence from Britain in 1960.
The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in 1983 in the north of the island, where more than 30,000 Turkish troops are still stationed. It is recognised only by Ankara.
